teaser.text: Kimberly-Clark makes the absorbent products people use to keep themselves, their children, their homes and their workplaces clean and dry. Its business looks simple at the shelf, but its money moves through brands, retailers, factories, suppliers and accounting boundaries.

stock.title: Kimberly-Clark stock forecast
stock.meta_description: Kimberly-Clark's stock forecast weighs China demand, Kenvue savings, cash generation, deleveraging and three valuation scenarios.
stock.opening: Kimberly-Clark's weighted forecast is $87.70 by October 2027 and $103.46 by October 2029. It hinges on China demand, Kenvue savings, cash generation and deleveraging.
stock.closing: The full Kimberly-Clark memo also answers how Kimberly-Clark works, who its rivals are, how management is executing, and which risks matter most.

blocks.heading: Where could Kimberly-Clark's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: Kimberly-Clark’s weighted path points to near-term downside followed by a modest recovery. The weighted price is $87.70 by October 2027, down 12% including dividends. It is $94.26 by October 2028, down 1%. By October 2029, it reaches $103.46, up 13%.

The bear-to-bull range by October 2029 runs from $63.41 to $155.69. Today’s price is $105.41. The bear case has a 32% probability, the base case 49%, and the bull case 19%, because the acquisition creates both meaningful synergy potential and substantial execution risk.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for Kimberly-Clark?

paragraphs.text: The base earnings row assumes revenue grows gradually and net margin improves from 11.3% to 12.1%. The bear case keeps revenue nearly flat and margins around 10%, because China weakness, pricing pressure, interest and integration disruption offset scale. The bull case raises revenue and margin more quickly, requiring China stabilization and prompt savings. Management targets $2.1 billion of annual benefits. It expects $2.5 billion of implementation costs during the first two years. Those facts support partial rather than immediate synergy delivery.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Kimberly-Clark really make?

paragraphs.text: Investment also rose. Continuing-business capital spending increased from $605 million in 2024 to $1,020 million in 2025. Stock pay was $130 million in 2025. It does not consume cash immediately, but it gives employees a claim on the company, so an owner-focused cash measure may deduct it.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay today for Kimberly-Clark?

paragraphs.text: At $105.41, a 20.1x trailing P/E implies $5.24 of trailing EPS. The 14.3x forward P/E implies $7.37 of future EPS. That forward denominator is roughly 41% higher, but the difference may reflect adjustments, reporting changes, and acquisition timing rather than underlying growth. At 12x, $7.37 of EPS supports roughly $88. To support $105.41 at that multiple requires $8.78 of EPS.

blocks.heading: How much does Kimberly-Clark pay its shareholders?

paragraphs.text: The dividend row rises modestly in the base case, freezes in the bear case and grows faster in the bull case. Kimberly-Clark paid $5.04 per share in 2025 and maintained a $1.28 quarterly rate in the first half of 2026. The five-year dividend growth rate was about 2.0% annually. The freeze remains credible because first-half cash left only $34 million after capital spending and common dividends.

blocks.heading: Does Kimberly-Clark's cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: Cash offers a further test. K-C generated about $0.9 billion of free cash flow in the first half of 2026 under a simple operating-cash-less-investment definition. Dividends consumed $843 million. That cash included discontinued operations, so the dividend is not proof that post-deal distributions will be comfortably funded.

The important pattern is that shareholder payments could exceed the simple free-cash-flow measure. When that happens, the company must draw down cash, borrow, sell assets or issue shares. Debt repayment also does not guarantee a stronger cushion: if cash falls faster than borrowings, net debt—debt minus cash—can rise.

blocks.heading: What has Kimberly-Clark guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: The retained business is still expected to deliver mid-single-digit adjusted operating-profit growth and high-single-digit adjusted EPS growth. Management also guides to US$2,000 million of adjusted free cash flow after capital spending, with gross productivity of 5.0%–6.0%. Gross productivity means savings before inflation, reinvestment and other costs reduce them. This guidance excludes Kenvue.

blocks.heading: Has Kimberly-Clark kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: The 2025 annual scorecard missed both disclosed targets. Organic sales growth was 1.1% against a 2.5% target, while adjusted earnings per share were $7.37 against $7.56. Organic growth removes currency and portfolio effects; adjusted earnings remove specified accounting items. Hsu’s annual incentive paid at 61% of target, and the committee excluded an accounting benefit from paused depreciation.

The longer-term award produced a different result. The 2023–2025 performance awards paid at 150% of target because organic growth met its goal and modified free cash flow exceeded its maximum. Modified free cash flow excluded transformation and separation cash costs. Those costs still reduce cash available to shareholders, so a weak annual award and a generous three-year payout can coexist.

blocks.heading: What do Kimberly-Clark’s last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: Revenue was $4,134 million, compared with $4,150 million a year earlier. Organic sales fell 1.3%. Gross margin declined from 36.0% to 34.9%. Operating income fell from $621 million to $516 million. Continuing diluted EPS nevertheless rose from $1.01 to $1.19 because earnings per share comes after taxes and other items.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Kimberly-Clark’s next results?

paragraphs.text: K-C plans to publish final third-quarter results and hold an analyst Q&A on November 5. The October 15 release was preliminary. Investors should look for a smaller China sales drag and profit improvement that does not depend on temporary help, since second-quarter adjusted results benefited from one-time tariff refunds.
